RESEARCH ARTICLE OPEN ACCESS
Seasonal Decomposition- Enhanced Deep Learning 
Architecture for Probabilistic Forecasting
Keyan Jin1 |  Francisco Javier Blanco-Encomienda 2
1International School for Postgraduate Studies, University of Granada, Granada, Spain | 2Faculty of Education, Economy and Technology, University of 
Granada, Ceuta, Spain
Correspondence:  Francisco Javier Blanco-  Encomienda ( jble@ugr.es)
Received:  15 April 2024 | Revised:  3 May 2024 | Accepted:  29 October 2025
Funding:  This work was supported by the Research Program from the Faculty of Education, Economy and Technology of Ceuta. Funding for open access 
charge: Universidad de Granada/CBUA.
Keywords: deep learning | financial markets | oil price | probabilistic forecasting | seasonal decomposition
ABSTRACT
Time series decomposition as a general preprocessing method has been widely used in the field of time series forecasting. 
However, since the future is unknown, this preprocessing practice is limited in realistic forecasting, especially in real-  time 
forecasting scenarios. In this paper, we propose a framework with time series decomposition and probabilistic forecasting capa -
bilities. Distinguishing from models based on time series pre-  decomposition, our proposed framework can decompose the series 
into trend components and seasonal components in real time to achieve end- to- end forecasting. We apply this framework to four 
state- of- the- art deep time series models and test their performance on four synthetic datasets and the WTI oil price dataset. The 
results show that the seasonal decomposition- based framework can significantly improve the point and probabilistic forecasting 
accuracy of the original models.
1   |   Introduction
Forecasting financial time series is a challenging task for two 
main reasons: (1) the complex nonlinearity.  When a source 
has both commodity and financial attributes, its price is not 
only affected by supply and demand but also greatly influ -
enced by other factors such as gross domestic product, stock 
market activities, foreign exchange rates, and even weather 
conditions (Bernabe et al.  2004 ; Tang et al.  2012; Yousefi and 
Wirjanto  2004 ). These factors may lead to a high degree of 
nonlinearity. Moreover, in the absence of a clear nonlinear 
relationship, large computational costs are consumed for in -
ference. (2) The complex temporal patterns. In general, time 
series can be regarded as a superposition of different mode 
functions or a combination of trend, seasonality and noise 
(Wen et al.  2021). The entanglement of multiple components 
may make the temporal pattern exhibit irregularity, reflected 
in unreliable and invisible dependencies. In response to these 
problems, researchers have developed many models over the 
past decades to capture the complex features of time series 
in order to effectively infer the future. In general, prediction 
models can be broadly classified into two categories: statisti -
cal models and machine learning models (Dastile et al.  2020 ; 
Jin et  al.  2023). Statistical models rely on stronger assump -
tions between the data and the model to estimate the explicit 
model structure and thus forecast, such as ARIMA, SARIMA, 
and so forth. Although these models have achieved superior 
predictive performance in some applications, they are ex -
pensive to use because the model assumptions require strong 
domain knowledge. Moreover, statistical models have lim -
ited nonlinear representation capability and perform poorly 
especially with massive data and features. Machine learning 
can be understood as a large-  scale optimization task that re -
sembles a functional optimization problem in its formulation, 
This is an open access article under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivs License, which permits use and distribution in any 
medium, provided the original work is properly cited, the use is non-commercial and no modifications or adaptations are made.

881
Journal of Forecasting, 2026
but is complex due to its large scale. Common machine learn -
ing models include support vector machine (SVM), gradient 
boosting tree (GBDT), artificial neural network (ANN), and so 
forth. Among them, neural network-  based deep learning (DL) 
techniques are widely studied and applied and gradually be -
come popular methods in the field of time series forecasting, 
such as LSTM (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber  1997), DeepTCN 
(Chen et al.  2020), TPA (Shih et al.  2019), and LogTrans (Li 
et  al.  2019a). Compared to classical statistical models, DL 
shows great potential in expressing complex nonlinear feature 
interactions, while the learning ability of DL has improved 
significantly compared to shallow neural networks and ma -
chine learning models in general (Lara-  Benítez et al. 2021 ).
Some research findings have shown the advantages of deep 
learning methods in prediction (Li et al.  2019b; Wu et al.  2021; 
Zhao et al.  2017), but they still have limitations for highly com -
plex financial data. In order to further reason about the intricate 
temporal patterns and improve the forecasting accuracy, some 
researchers have considered time series decomposition methods 
(Abdollahi 2020; Li et al. 2021). Based on the idea of “divide and 
conquer,” researchers decompose the time-  series into several 
simple components and solve the original complex problems 
by modeling these components separately. The decomposition 
methods usually contain two categories. The first class of meth -
ods treats the time series as a superposition of several different 
intrinsic mode functions, mainly including wavelet transform-  
based decomposition, empirical mode decomposition (EMD) 
and variational mode decomposition (VMD). Another class 
of approaches that treat time series as a combination of trend, 
seasonal, and residual components includes STL (Cleveland 
et al. 1990) and TBATS (De Livera et al. 2011).
Decomposition- based deep learning models have been shown 
to have more accurate predictive performance in fields such 
as finance and environment (Dong et al.  2021; Sun et al.  2021). 
However, these time series decomposition methods usually 
employ one- time decomposition strategies (OTDS), that is, de -
composition of all data containing both training data (historical 
data) and test data (future data) (Deng et al.  2020). In the con -
text of forecasting, the efficiency of this preprocessing practice 
is limited in real-  time forecasting scenarios because the future 
is unknown. In particular, the process of decomposing multiple 
series is tedious and time-  consuming in a multiseries forecast -
ing setting.
In this paper, we propose an end-  to- end deep learning frame -
work based on seasonal decomposition, which can be easily 
extended to various deep time series models. Our proposed 
framework supports probabilistic prediction functions, provid -
ing both parametric and non-  parametric methods. Extensive 
empirical studies have shown that our framework compares fa -
vorably with state-  of- the- art methods in both point prediction 
and probabilistic prediction tasks.
The four points considered in the proposed models compared to 
other models are as follows: (1) extremely fast series decomposi-
tion and fast training speed of the model; (2) high compatibility, 
as it is adaptable to various deep time series models; (3) nonlin -
ear capability; and (4) compatibility with point prediction and 
probabilistic prediction.
The remainder of this study is as follows. Section  2 briefly re -
views related literature on time series forecasting models, de -
composition methods and their combination. Section 3 describes 
the framework we proposed. Section  4 investigates the forecast -
ing performance of the models on different datasets. Section  5 
gives the conclusions.
2   |   Literature Review
Many research has applied deep learning methods in predic -
tions. For example, Bristone et al. (2020) present a hybrid model 
for forecasting that uses complex network analysis and long 
short- term memory (LSTM). The experiments showed that the 
proposed model has higher accuracy and is more robust and re -
liable. Chiroma et al. ( 2015) proposed an alternative approach 
based on a genetic algorithm and neural network (GA-  NN) for 
predictions. Based on the data transfer of prior knowledge, Cen 
and Wang (2019) empirically investigated the predictions effec -
tiveness using LSTM, whose result showed that LSTM with data 
transfer can greatly improve the prediction accuracy of compet -
ing models. Yang et al. ( 2021b) achieved good results by using 
multiscale data and kernel extreme learning machine (KELM) 
to make predictions. Recently, based on complexity theory, Lin 
et  al.  (2022) made predictions combining LSTM with Google 
Trends (GT). Their results explained the weak ability and dy -
namic impact of GT in improving the long- term forecasting.
To reduce modelling difficulty, the researchers apply decom -
position methods to transform the series into clear components 
and further model them with deep learning, which improve pre-
diction performance. For example, Jammazi and Aloui  ( 2012) 
combined Harr A trous wavelet decomposition and neural net -
work model to make predictions, and they found that the hy -
brid model has higher efficiency and higher accuracy in crude 
oil forecasting. Li et  al.  ( 2018) proposed an EEMD-  SBL- ADD 
model for forecastings by combining ensemble empirical mode 
decomposition (EEMD) and sparse Bayesian learning (SBL). 
Zhao et  al.  ( 2021) decomposed the series using an improved 
VMD method, whose parameters were optimized by the parti -
cle swarm according to the average maximum envelope entropy, 
and performed point prediction and interval prediction for the 
series. The interval prediction model was constructed based on 
the point prediction model and Bootstrap sampling.  Recently, 
Guo et  al.  ( 2022) decomposed the multi-  source series using 
VMD and fuzzy entropy (FE), then Granger causality test and 
random forest recursive feature elimination (RF-  RFE) were 
used to censor useful predictor variables. Finally, each recon -
struction mode was individually forecasted and the forecasting 
values obtained were combined and integrated. The empirical 
results showed that the proposed model improved the forecast -
ing accuracy. More literature based on decomposition and en -
semble forecasting frameworks can be found in (Salamai  2023; 
Sun et al. 2021; Sun et al. 2018).
Empirical studies have shown that the models can produce 
more accurate forecasts after de-  seasonalization of the time 
series. For example, Makridakis et  al.  ( 1982) used 68 monthly 
time series of M-  competition to compare the forecast perfor -
mance produced by NNs trained with de-  seasonalized and non- 
seasonalized data, and they found that the NNs trained with

early de-  seasonalization showed a significant improvement 
in forecasting accuracy. Yang et  al.  ( 2021a) proposed a Loess- 
based seasonal decomposition procedure combined with a one- 
dimensional convolutional neural network (STLeCNNePE) to 
predict the significant wave height, and their proposed model 
improved the prediction baseline. Zhang and Qi ( 2005)'s exper-
iments showed that NNs are not effective in directly modeling 
trends or seasonality, and emphasized that prediction errors can 
be reduced by detrending or deseasonalizing the original time 
series. Taieb et al. ( 2012) and Bandara et al. ( 2020) confirmed 
these findings.
3   |   Methodology
3.1   |   Problem Definition
A w-  horizon ahead probabilistic forecasting problem for time 
series can be described as follows. Given a set of time series y1:T , 
our goal is to model the conditional distribution of the future 
observation, denoted as 
where yt − k :t = /braceleft.s1yt − k , …, yt
/braceright.s1
 are observations of the target, 
xt− k :t = /braceleft.s1xt − k , …, xt
/braceright.s1
 are exogenous inputs (covariates) that can 
only be observed historically over a look-  back window and f ( ⋅ ) 
is the forecasting function learnt by the model. k is the length 
of the historical observations. In a broad sense, the deep neu -
ral networks used in time series forecasts are all sequence-  to- 
sequence (seq2seq) structures, that is, the encoder is used to 
encode historical information into latent states  h t, and then the 
decoder is used to convert h t and other information into outputs, 
namely: 
where genc ( ⋅ ) and gdec ( ⋅ ) are encoder and decoder, respectively. 
In a narrow sense, the model whose output is obtained only 
through the latent states h t does not have a decoder module (gen-
erally transformed through a simple nonlinear layer), and the 
model at this time no longer has a seq2seq structure.
3.2   |   Neural Network Architecture
In this paper, we propose an end-  to- end deep learning frame -
work based on seasonal decomposition for forecasting. The 
entire architecture of proposed framework is presented in 
Figure  1a. The high-  level architecture contains four layers. 
include seasonal decomposition layer, detrend layer, trend 
layer and probabilistic forecasting layer. In the seasonal

decomposition layer, the time series is first decomposed into 
a trend component and a detrend component, which is dom -
inated by seasonal components. And this is why this frame -
work is called seasonality-  based decomposition. Subsequently, 
the trend layer and detrend layer are used to mine potential 
features for these two components respectively to obtain la -
tent states hT  and hSR. Finally, a dense layer is applied to map 
the states and to produce the probabilistic forecasts of future 
observations. In the following sections, we provide further de -
tails for each layer.
3.2.1   |   Seasonal Decomposition Layer
Time series data can exhibit a variety of patterns. It is often 
helpful for prediction to decompose a time series into several 
components, each representing an underlying pattern cate -
gory. In this paper, the time series is considered as a combi -
nation of trend component, seasonal component and residual 
component, and in the case of additive decomposition, we can 
write 
We assume that the residual component is a white noise, so the 
time series can be reduced to two components, trend component 
and detrend component, denoted as 
In this paper, we apply a classical method of time series decom -
position, a moving average method to estimate the trend compo-
nent, which can be expressed as 
where m = 2k + 1. That is, the estimate of the trend at time t is 
obtained by averaging values of the time series within k periods. 
Observations that are nearby in time are also likely to be close in 
value. Therefore, the average eliminates some of the randomness 
in the data, leaving a smooth trend component. This is known as 
the m − MA process, meaning m- order moving average (Dagum 
and Bianconcini 2016).
We apply a series decomposition layer to achieve real-  time de -
composition of the time series (see Figure  1b). The time series 
is first complemented with first and last values to avoid missing 
values at both ends of the series due to the m − MA process, then 
the AvgPool layer is applied to simulate the m − MA process by 
which we obtain the trend component, and finally the detrend 
component is obtained from the difference between the original 
series and the trend component.
3.2.2   |   Detrend Layer
Four representative modules are used as detrend layers to 
mine the temporal and inter-  variate interaction charac -
teristics of the detrend components: two attention-  based 
models, LogSparse Transformer (LogTrans) (Li et  al.  2019a) 
and Temporal Pattern Attention (TPA) (Shih et  al.  2019), 
one RNN-  based model, Long Short-  Term Memory network 
(LSTM) (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber  1997), and CNN-  based 
Temporal Convolutional network (TCN) (Bai et al.  2018). With 
the detrend layer, the latent state of the detrend component hSR
t  
can be obtained.
3.2.3   |   Trend Layer
The Conv1D layer is first applied to smooth the trend compo -
nents and mine the interaction features between variables. 
Then, the t- step outputs of the Conv1D layer are reduced to 1 
using the dense layer, which is similar to the autoregressive 
model. With the trend layer, latent state of the trend component 
hT
t  can be obtained.
3.2.4   |   Probabilistic Forecasting Layer
We consider two probabilistic forecasting methods in this 
paper. The first one is a parametric method. It requires a pre- 
assumed probability distribution (e.g., Gaussian distribution), 
based on the negative log-  likelihood loss, to achieve probabi -
listic forecasts of future observations. Since it directly forecasts 
the parameters of the assumed distribution, it allows flexibility 
to obtain additional information by sampling from the esti -
mated distribution. The second one is a nonparametric method. 
Based on the quantile loss, it allows the model to output a set 
of forecasts corresponding to the quantile points of interest. 
This method is distribution-  free and therefore usually more ro -
bust. Specifically, in the probabilistic forecasting layer, hT
t  and 
hSR
t  are first summed as the latent output of the historical time 
series, and then, the dense layer is used to generate m outputs 
Z = (h1 ,⋯ ,hm ), which represent the parameters of the hypo -
thetical distribution of interest.
For the parametric method, we assume that the time series fol -
lows a Gaussian distribution, and for the future observation yt+1, 
the probabilistic forecasting layer produces H t+1 = (/u1D707t+1 ,/u1D70Et+1 ), 
where /u1D707t+1 is the expected value and /u1D70Et+1 is the standard devi -
ation of yt+1. Then, the negative log-  likelihood function is con -
structed as a loss function: 
In addition, to ensure that the standard deviation of the prob -
abilistic forecasting layer satisfies the positivity condition 
(Chen et al.  2020; Salinas et al.  2020), we use the SoftReLU ac -
tivation function for the standard deviation, which is denoted 
as z = log(1 + exp(z)).
For the nonparametric method, forecasts can be obtained by 
quantile regression. The observation and forecasts of a specific 
quantile level q are denoted as y and ̂y, respectively, and the 
q- quantile is defined as

3.3   |   Performance Evaluation Criteria
For out- of- sample testing, we evaluate the normalized quantile 
losses across the entire forecasting horizon- focusing on P50 risk, 
which is denoted as 
where Lq( ⋅ ) is defined in Equation ( 7), Ω is the domain of test 
data, and q = 0. 5. Root mean square error (RMSE) is used in our 
experiments for point forecasting, which is denoted as 
where yt is the true value at time step t and /uni0302.s1yt is the correspond-
ing prediction value.
3.4   |   Datasets
3.4.1   |   Synthetic Datasets
To generate the synthetic dataset, we incorporate different types 
of seasonality, trend changes, and noise to simulate real- world sce-
narios, as shown in Figure 2. Specifically, we generate two types of 
seasonal components. For a periodic signal, the first one (Uniform) 
follows a uniform distribution yt ∼ U ( − 1, 1), and the second one 
(Wave) has a square wave- like shape, which is denoted as 
The seasonal period T is set to 25, and a total of 10,000 time 
points are generated. In addition, this paper randomly se -
lects 10 moments and randomly rises or falls by 1 unit at the 
corresponding moment to form the first trend component 
(Random) and rises by 1 unit at each selected moment to form 
the second trend component (Rise). Four synthetic datasets 
are generated by combining seasonal and trend components 
two-  by- two (see Figure  2). The noise is added by the standard 
normal distribution.

ties may affect the crude oil prices (Wang et  al.  2015; Zhao 
et al.  2017), we collect the CBOE DJIA Volatility Index (VIX),

trade-  weighted dollar index (TWUSDX) to construct the mul -

Table  1 shows the descriptive statistics for the WTI crude oil 
price dataset, from which it can be seen that WTI crude oil prices 
have a positive skewness (0.35) and a kurtosis value of −0.75, and 
the Jarque- Bera statistic rejects the hypothesis of normal distri -
bution at 1% confidence level. The Ljung-  Box test results of the 
5th- , 10th- , and 20th-  order lagged terms indicate that oil prices 
have significant autocorrelation characteristics, which indicates 
the long memory nature in the crude oil spot market. The ADF 
statistic indicates that series is not smooth.
4   |   Results
We selected the four models mentioned in Section  3.2.2  as the 
baseline and used them to forecast the target values for the 
next 10 moments. In addition, to distinguish from these base -
line methods, we wrote the series decomposition-  based model 
as Model- De. All datasets were divided according to 0.7:0.1:0.2 
without disrupting the chronological order. All models were 
trained using the Adam optimizer (Kingma and Ba  2014) 
with an initial learning rate of 10e-3. Batch size was set to 
32. The training process was early stopped within 50 epochs. 
All experiments were repeated three times, implemented in 
P yTorch.
4.1   |   Results on Synthetic Datasets
For the synthetic dataset, we performed forecasting for 10 future 
time points using the series length of the last 50 (containing two 
periods) and evaluated the probabilistic forecasting performance of 
our proposed framework using the q- risk of 0.5 and 0.9 quantiles. 
It should be noted that for the parametric probabilistic forecasting 
model, Gaussian distributions corresponding to the forecasting pa-
rameters (mean and standard deviation) were generated and used 
to compute the 0.5 and 0.9 quantile forecasting values. In addition, 
we evaluated the point forecasting performance using RMSE.
Tables 2, 3, and 4 show the parametric probability, nonparamet-
ric probability, and point prediction performance of the model 
on the four synthetic datasets, respectively. We label the top

on Wave-  Random data than on other synthetic datasets due

seasonal decomposition-  based models perform better at almost 
all forecast moments for all synthetic datasets.
4.2   |   Results on WTI Crude Oil Price Dataset
The probabilistic forecasting results of WTI-  MS and WTI-  S 
are shown in Tables  5 and 6 . We can find that the seasonal 
decomposition- based models achieve better forecasting results 
compared to the original models. From the forecasting per -
formance of the 0.5 quantile, the nonparametric probabilistic 
models do not show significant dominance over the parametric 
probabilistic model. However, the forecasting results for the 0.9 
quantile show the superiority of the nonparametric approach. 
For presentation purposes, the results for the 0.9 quantile are 
not given, and a supporting evidence can be seen from Figure  3. 
One possible reason for this is that parametric probabilistic fore-
casting models are constructed based on Gaussian distributions, 
but as Table 1 shows, the WTI crude oil price does not follow this 
assumption. In contrast, the nonparametric probabilistic fore -
casting models, which take into account the distribution-  free 
nature, produce better forecasts by directly minimizing quan -
tile loss.
To better understand the performance improvement of the pro -
posed framework, we show the probabilistic forecasting results 
of the LSTM and LSTM-  De for the WTI- MS dataset a- day ahead 
in Figure  3, where the top and the bottom subplot are the para -
metric and non-  probabilistic results, respectively. Comparing 
the nonparametric probabilistic performance of LSTM and 
LSTM- De, see Figure  3c,d, we can find that the target value 
is always within the 0.1 and 0.9 quantile prediction range of 
LSTM- De, while the prediction interval of LSTM can only track 
the trend of the target value. In addition, comparing the results

of probability prediction based on Gaussian distribution with 
those based on quantile loss, the results of nonparametric proba-
bility prediction are more accurate, and this finding is consistent 
with the performance of the models on synthetic datasets.
Table 7 shows the point forecasting performance of the model 
on the WTI-  MS and WTI-  S datasets. As can be seen, our pro -
posed seasonal decomposition-  based framework is still valid, 
and it improves the forecasting performance of almost all base -
line models. In addition, there is no accuracy gain in WTI crude 
oil price forecasting by adding additional exogenous variables. 
To illustrate the high performance of the proposed framework, 
we plot the point forecasting error distribution of the models for 
the WTI-  MS dataset in Figure  4. It can be found that the per -
formance of the models become worse as the predicted moment 
is extended, and the error distribution of Model-  De is around 0, 
while the corresponding original model error deviates from 0 
and its dispersion is higher.
5   |   Conclusion
We present an end-  to- end deep learning framework based on 
seasonal decomposition for probabilistic forecasting that sup -
ports both nonparametric and parametric methods to model 
probabilistic distributions. Distinguishing from models based 
on time series pre-  decomposition, our proposed framework is 
end- to- end. And since it models the trend component and the 
seasonal component separately, the framework can be adapted 
to various deep time series models.

890
 Journal of Forecasting, 2026
To test the forecasting ability of the proposed framework, we 
first construct four synthetic datasets containing different sea -
sonal and trend components to verify the compatibility of the 
framework for forecasting different types of time series. On this 
basis, we further use it to forecast the WTI crude oil prices.
The results of five datasets show that the deep time series model 
based on seasonal decomposition yields superior performance 
compared to original neural network model in both point and 
probabilistic forecasting.
